opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've been thinking about for a long time, and my honest view is that we're not there yet. Understanding and generation in the visual domain are still largely two separate systems, even when they look unified from the outside.

In language, GPT got something remarkable almost for free: when you train a model to predict the next token, generation and understanding are the same thing. If you can continue a text well, you've understood it, and that understanding then improves your generation. They form a closed loop that reinforces itself. That's why scaling worked so cleanly for language.

In vision, we haven't found that loop. Many people have tried to put understanding and generation into one model, and I've done some of this work myself. Technically you can make it work: one transformer that both describes images and produces them. But when you look carefully, the two capabilities don't really help each other. Adding generation data doesn't clearly improve understanding, and adding understanding data doesn't clearly improve generation. Sometimes they even compete. So it's unification in architecture, not in capability. It's two models sharing a body.

I think the root cause is that we haven't found the right objective for vision. Next-token prediction works for language because language is already highly abstract and compressed. Every token carries meaning, so predicting it forces you to model semantics. Pixels are different. Most of the information in an image is low-level texture and detail, so if you train a model to reconstruct pixels, most of its capacity goes into things that don't matter for understanding. Diffusion models generate beautiful images, but that doesn't mean they "understand" in the sense we care about, like reasoning about what's happening or what will happen next.

So for the next multimodal GPT, a few things have to come together.

First, the representation. We need visual tokens or latents that are both semantic enough to support reasoning and complete enough to reconstruct the image. Today's tokenizers usually make a trade-off: either they're good for reconstruction and weak semantically, or the reverse. Resolving that tension is, I think, a foundational problem.

Second, and more important, the data and the task. In language, the internet gives us text where the next token is naturally predictable from context. For vision, I think the natural analogue may be video, or more precisely, sequences where the next frame or state follows causally from what came before. If a model has to predict what happens next in the world, not just the pixels but the consequences of actions, then generation starts to require understanding. That's where the closed loop could come back.

Third, reasoning. We've seen in language that once you add long chain-of-thought and reinforcement learning, the model's capability changes qualitatively. I suspect vision needs something similar: the ability to "think" in a visual or multimodal space, maybe generating intermediate images or sketches as part of reasoning, the way a person might draw a diagram to solve a geometry problem. When generation becomes a tool for thinking rather than just an output, that's when I'd say understanding and generation are truly unified.

So my vision of the next multimodal GPT is not just a model that can both caption and draw. It's a model where generating the world and understanding the world are the same process, and each one makes the other stronger. We haven't found the recipe yet, but I think the pieces are starting to appear: better tokenizers, large-scale video, and reasoning with RL. Whoever combines them in the right way might have the multimodal equivalent of the GPT moment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key realization is that generation and understanding are not two problems — they're one problem seen from two sides. When you look at how language models work, next-token prediction is simultaneously a generative task and a comprehension task. You can't predict the next word well unless you understand the preceding text. That unification is why LLMs became so powerful. Vision hasn't had that yet. Historically we had CLIP-style models for understanding and diffusion models for generation, trained on different objectives, with different representations, and the two camps barely talked to each other.

So when I imagine the next multimodal GPT, the first thing I want is a shared representation space where visual tokens play the same role as text tokens. Not a vision encoder bolted onto a language model through a projection layer, which is what most current VLMs do, but a truly native representation where the model can both read images and write them using the same machinery. The question is what that visual token should be. Discrete VQ-style tokens are attractive because they fit autoregressive training cleanly, but they lose information and the reconstruction quality has a ceiling. Continuous latents, as in diffusion, preserve detail but don't fit the next-token framework naturally. I think the answer is probably a hybrid — autoregressive modeling over coarse semantic structure, with some form of continuous or diffusion-based refinement for fine detail. Several groups are exploring this, and I don't think the final form is settled.

The second thing, and this is the part I care more about, is the training objective. In language, the objective is trivially aligned with understanding because text is already a compressed, semantic signal. Pixels aren't. If you just do next-pixel or next-patch prediction, most of the model's capacity gets spent on low-level texture and noise that carries no semantic information. So I think the model needs something like a hierarchy of prediction targets — predicting semantics before predicting appearance. In a sense this is what happens when you train on interleaved image-text data: the text acts as a semantic anchor that forces the visual representation to be meaningful. But I'd like the model to learn that structure even without text supervision, because the amount of unlabeled video in the world dwarfs any captioned dataset.

Which brings me to the third point: video is the real target, not static images. Images are a degenerate case. Video has temporal structure, causality, physical consistency — if you can predict the next frames of a video well, you have to have learned something about how the world works, about objects, about dynamics. That's what people mean by a world model. I think the next multimodal GPT, done properly, is implicitly a world model, and generation becomes the way the model does reasoning about the physical world, the same way chain-of-thought is how an LLM reasons about abstract problems. You "imagine" the consequence of an action by generating it.

I want to be honest about what we don't know, though. There's a fundamental tension: generation wants to model the full data distribution, including all the irrelevant variation, while understanding wants to throw that variation away. Whether one network can do both without one objective hurting the other is still an empirical question. Early unified models have generally been worse than specialized ones at both tasks. My bet is that this is a scaling and data problem rather than a fundamental one, the same way early multitask language models looked worse than specialists until they didn't. But I could be wrong, and it's possible the right architecture ends up with distinct pathways that share a semantic core rather than being fully unified. Either way, I think the next couple of years will tell us, because the compute is finally there to run the experiment at scale.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make generation and understanding reinforce each other within one model. Today, we often treat them as separate tasks: one system interprets an image, and another produces an image from a description. A more unified model would learn both what a scene contains and how its elements fit together well enough to create or modify it.

For example, you could show it a room, discuss why the layout feels cramped, and ask it to visualize a better arrangement. It would need to preserve the room’s geometry, understand your constraints, and make changes that match its explanation. That requires more than connecting an image generator to a language model.

The open question is how much of the representation and training objective should be shared. Understanding benefits from abstraction, while generation needs to retain fine visual detail. I don’t think unification necessarily means forcing everything into an identical format. It means those capabilities work together coherently, so the model can explain what it generates and generate what it understands.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make generation and understanding reinforce each other. When a model looks at an image, it should understand the objects, their relationships, and the structure of the scene. When it generates or edits an image, it should use that same understanding to control what changes and what stays consistent.

For example, you could show it a room and ask, “What would this look like with the sofa beside the window?” It would need to understand the layout, reason about the move, and generate a plausible result. You could then ask why it placed something there, or refine the image through conversation.

The interesting question is whether a shared representation can support both tasks without sacrificing the strengths of either. Visual understanding often benefits from abstraction, while generation requires preserving fine detail. I would expect a unified system to connect those levels, rather than assume that one representation automatically solves everything.
